title: Landline retirement day: what we can learn from the FAA outage
summary: A copper line replacement took down the FAA’s network. Learn what the outage teaches about landline retirement and keeping your home phone working.
body_markdown:
On Friday, November 13, a crew at a remote FAA site was swapping out old copper communication lines for new fiber equipment. That equipment turned out to be faulty.


Picture a phone that rings 1,000 times every few seconds, so you can never answer anyone else. That’s what a new router did to the FAA’s system, and air traffic controllers started losing their radio and radar connections. So the FAA stopped every departing flight in the United States.


At Community Phone, we think few things matter more than a reliable connection to family, friends, and care providers. That’s why we wanted to see what this outage could teach us. Here’s what we found.


## Your landline runs on copper, too


Most traditional landlines run on the same kind of copper wire, and phone companies are replacing those lines across the country.[AT&T](https://www.communityphone.org/switch-from-att) plans to retire most of its copper network by the end of 2029.[Verizon](https://www.communityphone.org/switch-from-verizon) is moving customers from copper to fiber.[CenturyLink](https://www.communityphone.org/switch-from-centurylink) is retiring copper service in selected areas and offering replacement options.


The FAA has a $22 billion budget and engineers on call, and a routine copper replacement still brought its network down. The same kind of replacement is now happening in people’s homes, with none of the same resources or oversight. Few days will put your phone service at greater risk than the day your landline is replaced.


## Lesson 1: A single failing router shouldn’t take out your service


The FAA’s system had one weak point. When a single new piece of equipment malfunctioned in one place, the whole network went down, and there was nothing to fall back on.


A home phone can have the same weak point. Many landline replacements run over your home internet, so your phone depends on that one connection. When the internet goes down, the phone goes with it. If that’s your only phone, you can’t even call to report the outage.


### How Community Phone solves it


Community Phone’s Phone Base doesn’t need internet or traditional phone lines. When you have an internet outage, your phone keeps working.


Community Phone uses industrial-grade antennas to connect to the strongest local phone tower. If that tower has trouble, the Base can switch to another tower nearby.


## Lesson 2: An “upgrade” can take away something that used to work


The FAA’s replacement added a piece of equipment the old copper never needed. Many home phone replacements do the same thing.


Traditional landlines do a lot of things well. They’re simple to use, they often keep working when the power goes out, and people tend to keep the same phone and number for decades.


A replacement can change all of that. Many landline alternatives need power from your home. Some also come with complicated new equipment to learn and take care of.


### How Community Phone solves it


The Phone Base has a built-in backup battery that keeps your phone connected for up to 26 hours when the power goes out.


Most things stay the same: You can keep the phone you already have, and you can keep the same number, too. We’ll even help you transfer it. You can keep dialing and answering the phone the same simple way you always have. There’s nothing new to learn.


## Lesson 3: You shouldn’t have to wait for a technician


The FAA relied on a contractor to replace its old copper lines, and simply had to trust that everything went perfectly. Unfortunately for travelers around the country, it didn’t.


Many landline replacements work the same way. A technician handles the switch, which usually means you have to schedule an appointment and wait for them to come. It can take weeks, and the wait starts over if something goes wrong with the installation.


### How Community Phone solves it


You set up Community Phone yourself; we’ll mail it straight to your home. Just plug the Phone Base into a power outlet, connect the phone you already have to the Base, and listen for the dial tone. There’s no technician and no appointment. It usually takes about two minutes.


If you ever need help, a real person answers the phone in under two minutes on average.


## Don’t wait for your own November 13


Despite what happened on November 13, the FAA is still going to replace the rest of its copper lines. Air traffic controllers will rely on that new equipment for many years to come.


Whatever replaces your landline will be the phone you use every day. If it stops working, it won’t get the same emergency response as an FAA outage. You’ll still need it, but you’ll have to wait for your phone company to fix it on their schedule.


If you want a home phone that just works when your landline is gone, find out if Community Phone covers your address.
